strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated by prior interpretability findings (Zhou et al., 2024) that LLMs internally learn Fourier-like features for numbers, and is backed by clean theoretical justification (Lemma 3.3/3.4) showing exact digit recoverability via modular arithmetic on circular embeddings.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple arithmetic tasks (addition, subtraction, multiplication, decimal arithmetic, modular arithmetic, binary classification) with strong and consistent results: FoNE is the only method achieving 100% accuracy on over 100K test examples across several tasks, with substantial data efficiency (64x less data) and parameter efficiency gains over subword/digit-wise tokenization and xVal.

Thorough ablation studies (choice of periods, necessity of sine/cosine vs. direct digit encoding, linear projection vs. zero padding) that support the design choices with concrete failure-mode analysis (e.g., mod5 confusing digits 2 and 7).

Demonstrates scalability beyond the main synthetic benchmarks: 60-digit addition via chunking, combination with Abacus positional embeddings for length generalization, and comparison against a more recent competitive baseline (Number Token Loss), where FoNE substantially outperforms all NTL variants.

Provides evidence that FoNE does not harm (and can even improve) general language modeling ability via GPT-2 pretraining on FineWeb and continual pretraining of Llama-3.1-1B, addressing a natural concern about integrating a specialized numerical embedding into general-purpose LMs.

Good engineering detail and reproducibility: explicit algorithms in the appendix, discussion of practical integration (numeric parsers, [NUM] token), and a discussion section addressing several natural design questions (why classification loss, why base 10, why FoNE outperforms other embeddings).
weaknesses: The primary empirical validation remains on synthetic, controlled arithmetic tasks with small operand ranges (up to 6 digits) and small-to-medium models trained from scratch; there is limited evidence of benefit on realistic downstream numerical reasoning tasks (e.g., GSM8K, MATH, real quantitative reasoning benchmarks) beyond a narrow arithmetic slice of Brown et al. (2020) and MMLU (which shows no meaningful improvement, only no degradation).

The continual pretraining experiment uses a 'simplified' version of FoNE that differs substantially from the full proposed method (building on top of BPE tokens and learning only a projection layer rather than overriding embeddings and the special [NUM] token/decoding scheme), suggesting the full method may be difficult to integrate into existing pretrained LLMs and undermining claims of general applicability to LLM pretraining.

The decoding mechanism requires a special [NUM] token and a bespoke digit-wise classification head, which is a nontrivial architectural change to standard LM generation/decoding and is not evaluated in the more realistic pretraining-from-scratch-on-FineWeb setting for actual arithmetic performance (only perplexity is reported there, not arithmetic accuracy or generation quality on numeric outputs).

The method has intrinsic limitations for large numbers (float64 precision ceiling requiring chunking into 5-digit groups), and the effectiveness of this chunking heuristic is only demonstrated on one synthetic 60-digit addition setting rather than more diverse or naturally occurring long-number scenarios.

The core novelty is largely in directly operationalizing an already-known interpretability insight (Fourier features naturally emerge in pretrained LLMs) rather than a fundamentally new representational idea; the technical contribution is incremental relative to Zhou et al. (2024) and related sinusoidal/DICE/SALSA works, mainly differing in choosing digit-aligned base-10 periods and a parallel decoding scheme.

Some baseline comparisons could be strengthened - e.g., limited justification that hyperparameters (learning rates, epochs) for digit-wise/subword/xVal/NTL baselines were tuned as extensively as FoNE, and the WikiTableQuestions token-efficiency claim is a single anecdotal statistic rather than a broader real-world task evaluation.

strengths: The core idea—encoding each digit as a 2D sinusoidal (cos/sin) feature at digit-aligned periods (10^i)—is simple, clearly motivated by prior interpretability findings (Zhou et al., 2024), and comes with an elementary but clean theoretical justification (recoverability of x mod T from sin/cos pairs, and robustness to LayerNorm/RMSNorm scaling).

The empirical evaluation is unusually extensive for this type of paper: synthetic arithmetic (addition, subtraction, multiplication, modular arithmetic, binary classification), 60-digit addition via chunking, combination with Abacus embeddings, comparison against many baselines (digit-wise, subword/BPE, xVal, NTL, fine-tuned Llama-3.2-1B), and two attempts at integrating with pretrained/pretraining-from-scratch LLMs (continual pretraining on Llama-3.1 and GPT-2 pretraining on FineWeb).
Thorough ablations (linear projection vs. zero-padding, choice of periods/bases, necessity of sinusoidal vs. direct digit encoding) help isolate why the design choices matter.

Efficiency claims (token count, training/inference time, data efficiency) are concretely quantified and benchmarked against reasonable baselines, and the method is shown to be compatible with other positional schemes (Abacus).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the central mechanism (digit-wise multi-frequency Fourier/sinusoidal embeddings) is closely related to prior numeracy-preserving embeddings (xVal, DICE, SALSA) and to the interpretability work it is explicitly built on (Zhou et al. 2024); the main contribution is largely an engineering realization of an already-observed phenomenon rather than a fundamentally new representational idea.

The method requires pre-specifying maximum integer/decimal digit lengths (m, n) as global hyperparameters, which is a significant practical limitation for general-purpose LLMs that must handle numbers of unknown or highly variable magnitude; the chunking workaround for very large numbers (Section 4.4/Appendix F) does not restore perfect accuracy (97.42%) and adds complexity.

The real-world/LLM-integration evidence is thin and somewhat inconsistent with the main method: continual pretraining on Llama-3.1 uses a 'simplified' FoNE variant (built on top of BPE subwords rather than replacing number tokens entirely) because the full method is apparently hard to integrate into an existing tokenizer/vocabulary, which undercuts the claim that FoNE can be seamlessly incorporated into pretrained LLMs.

Downstream/validation evidence beyond synthetic arithmetic is weak: the FineWeb pretraining experiment only reports perplexity (a modest improvement, 46.8 vs 48.7 for the next best) and MMLU scores (38.10% vs 38.21%, a negligible difference) rather than any real numeracy-dependent downstream task (e.g., GSM8K, numerical QA, table reasoning accuracy), so claims about 'significant implications for pre-training LLMs' are not well substantiated at meaningful scale.

The paper's claim of being 'the only method that achieves 100% accuracy' is weakened by its own results—multiplication accuracy is not perfect even for FoNE (98.56%, 99.95%, 89.3% in different tables), and the abstract/intro oversell the generality of the perfect-accuracy claims relative to what is actually shown across all tasks and scales.

Most reported results lack variance/error bars or multiple-seed statistics (only the Abacus combination experiment uses 3 seeds), making it hard to assess the robustness and statistical significance of the comparisons, especially given many baseline methods (e.g., XVAL, NTL-S) collapse to near-zero accuracy in ways that seem almost like implementation/tuning artifacts rather than fundamental limitations.

The decoding head and loss (fixed 10-way classification per digit position, independent of global embedding dimension d) is a nontrivial departure from standard LM heads, and its integration overhead/compatibility with a full open-vocabulary LLM (beyond the simplified continual-pretraining setup) is not rigorously analyzed.
Minor presentation issues (e.g., duplicated row in Table 11, dense notation) somewhat reduce clarity and polish.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated by interpretability findings (Zhou et al. 2024), and technically clean: encoding each digit via sin/cos pairs at periods 10^i gives a compact, single-token, frequency-agnostic representation with a lightweight theoretical justification (Lemma 3.3/3.4) for exact digit recoverability.

Extensive empirical validation across many axes: multiple arithmetic tasks (addition, subtraction, multiplication, decimal, modular arithmetic, binary classification), model-size and data-size scaling curves, comparisons against digit-wise, subword, xVal, NTL, and fine-tuned Llama-3.2-1B baselines, and training/inference efficiency measurements.
Strong and consistent results: FoNE is often the only method reaching 100% accuracy, needs far less data/parameters, and is faster in training/inference than digit-wise and subword baselines.

Good ablations addressing natural design questions (linear vs zero-padding projection, choice of periods/bases, necessity of sinusoidal vs raw digit encoding, comparison with NTL) that strengthen the design justification.

Demonstrates broader applicability beyond synthetic arithmetic: combination with Abacus embeddings for length generalization to 50-digit numbers, chunking strategy enabling 60-digit addition in one pass, integration into continual pretraining of Llama-3.1-1B and from-scratch GPT-2 pretraining on FineWeb showing no (and sometimes positive) impact on language modeling perplexity/MMLU.

The paper is generally clearly written with helpful figures (Fig 1, 2, 6) illustrating the encoding/decoding pipeline, and provides a reasonability formal proof for the key recoverability lemma plus a LayerNorm/RMSNorm invariance lemma explaining why FoNE is more robust than magnitude-based alternatives like xVal.
weaknesses: Scope of tasks remains narrow: nearly all main results are on synthetic, single-operation arithmetic (fixed-length addition/subtraction/multiplication) rather than more realistic tasks combining numbers with broader reasoning or multi-step composition, so it's unclear how well gains transfer to real downstream numerical reasoning tasks beyond the small WikiTableQuestions token-count anecdote.

Requires knowing m and n (max integer/decimal digit lengths) as fixed global hyperparameters ahead of time, and numbers longer than 15 digits require manual chunking (Section 4.4/Appendix F) — this limits plug-and-play generality for open-ended pretraining corpora where number lengths are highly variable and not known a priori.

The decoding head (Definition 3.6/3.7) predicts each digit independently as a 10-way classification, which could in principle produce inconsistent/invalid combinations of digits (no explicit carry-consistency mechanism), and the paper doesn't discuss failure modes or error analysis for the residual errors (e.g., the 98.56%/89.3% multiplication accuracy cases).

The large-scale pretraining evidence (Section 5, Q4) is relatively limited in scale (117M GPT-2 on 10B tokens, continual pretraining of a 1B model) and uses a 'simplified' FoNE variant for the LLM integration, which is a reasonable pragmatic choice but somewhat weakens the direct connection between the theoretical claims and the pretrained-LLM experiments; larger-scale or more diverse LLM integration experiments would strengthen the significance claims.

Some comparisons (e.g., against very recent frontier LLMs like GPT-5/Qwen3-235B in Appendix E.1, and NTL baselines) are useful context but not deeply analyzed (e.g., no discussion of why NTL-subword fails so catastrophically beyond noting it, or why FoNE's improvement over NTL-digit is so large despite conceptual similarity).

The choice of base-10 periods is somewhat ad hoc/empirically motivated (mirroring what LLMs already learn) rather than derived from a principled optimality argument, though the paper does provide some ablations (Table 3, Table 6/7) to partially justify this.
